assessment.Interference with freedom of expression: The disciplinary proceedings and the sanction consisting of a 5% salary reduction for two months clearly amounted to an interference with the applicant’s freedom of expression under Article 10, as they were imposed because of two Facebook posts published on his personal account with around 50,000 followers (see paragraphs 16, 26 and 41).

assessment.Prescribed by law and legitimate aim: The interference was likely based on a sufficiently accessible domestic legal framework, notably Articles 90 and 99(a) of Law no. 303/2004, as interpreted by the domestic courts and the Constitutional Court (see paragraphs 32-33, 40, 43 and 49). It also pursued a legitimate aim, namely maintaining the authority and impartiality of the judiciary and protecting the image of the justice system (see paragraphs 33-35). The decisive issue is therefore whether the interference was 'necessary in a democratic society'.

assessment.Applicable Article 10 standard for judge: The Court accepts that judges are subject to duties of restraint and discretion, but any restriction on their speech calls for close scrutiny, especially where they speak on matters of public interest concerning democracy, the rule of law or the justice system. In particular, judges do not lose Article 10 protection when participating, as citizens, in debate on constitutional matters or judicial independence (see no. 28396/95; see no. 29492/05).

assessment.Context and public-interest nature of th: Both impugned posts concerned matters of very high public interest. The first was posted in the context of a public institutional dispute over the extension of the Army Chief of Staff’s term of office and referred to constitutional democracy and the risk of political control over key institutions (see paragraphs 17-18 and 23). The second endorsed an interview by a prosecutor criticising legislative reforms, the handling of criminal cases, and pressure on judges and prosecutors (see paragraph 19). The applicant was a well-known judge active in public debates on democracy, the rule of law and the justice system (see paragraph 14). This context strongly increases the level of protection under Article 10.

assessment.Assessment of the first post: The first message was provocative and capable of being misunderstood, especially its rhetorical reference to the army 'out on the streets' defending democracy (see paragraph 17). Still, read in context, it appears to have been political-constitutional commentary rather than a literal call for military intervention or unlawful action. The applicant expressly stated that it was neither a warning nor a call to disobey the law, but a comment linked to an ongoing public debate on the Army Chief of Staff’s appointment (see paragraph 23). The domestic bodies focused mainly on possible public interpretations and media headlines, rather than on the post’s actual meaning, context and intent (see paragraphs 27-29 and 37-39).

assessment.Assessment of the second post: The second message, although informal in tone, was essentially an expression of support for another magistrate speaking publicly about problems affecting the justice system (see paragraphs 19 and 21). The phrase 'some blood in his veins' was colloquial and arguably unbecoming for a judge, but it was not obscene, threatening or hateful. Taken alone, that wording seems insufficient to justify disciplinary liability, especially as the underlying topic was again judicial independence and criminal-justice policy, both matters of public concern (see paragraphs 19, 23 and 36).

assessment.Deficiencies in the domestic courts’ bal: The domestic authorities gave decisive weight to the applicant’s duty of discretion and to the adverse media reaction, but they did not convincingly show a pressing social need for sanctioning him. They treated his statements as 'defamatory allegations' or as inherently damaging to the image of the judiciary, yet the High Court explicitly refused to assess whether the allegations had any factual basis (see paragraphs 28, 38 and 76). It also relied heavily on how media and online comments interpreted the posts (see paragraphs 37 and 39), even though third-party distortion should not by itself determine the limits of the applicant’s freedom of expression. The dissent within the Disciplinary Board further shows that the domestic assessment was not self-evident and that an outright restriction on critical comments by judges on matters of public interest risks being excessive (see paragraph 29).

assessment.Public confidence and actual harm: The authorities asserted that the posts impaired public confidence in the judiciary because they were widely shared and discussed (see paragraphs 28-29 and 39-41). However, there was no concrete demonstration of actual damage beyond public controversy itself. Article 10 protects speech that shocks, offends or disturbs, especially in public debate. The applicant did not comment on pending proceedings contrary to Article 10 of Law no. 303/2004, nor did he disclose confidential information or attack litigants in a case before him (see paragraph 43). These factors reduce the weight of the justification for restricting his speech.

assessment.Proportionality and chilling effect: Although the sanction was relatively mild in quantitative terms, it remained a formal disciplinary penalty imposed on a sitting judge for participating in debate on democratic governance and judicial matters (see paragraphs 26 and 41). Such a measure is capable of producing a chilling effect, not only on the applicant but also on other judges and prosecutors who may wish to speak out on rule-of-law issues. That is particularly significant where the applicant was known for civic engagement and where broader concerns existed about disciplinary action against magistrates critical of reforms (see paragraphs 14, 15, 71 and 72).

assessment.Overall conclusion: In light of the high public-interest value of the speech, the absence of comments on pending cases, the insufficiently nuanced assessment of context and intent, the excessive reliance on reputational concerns and media amplification, and the chilling effect of disciplinary punishment, the domestic authorities did not provide relevant and sufficient reasons capable of showing that the interference was necessary in a democratic society. Applying the Court’s approach in cases concerning judges speaking on constitutional and judicial matters (see no. 28396/95; see no. 29492/05), it is likely that Article 10 was violated.
